en: The Treatise on the Causes and Conditions of Pratyekabuddhas, Volume One.
Translator’s name lost; now appended to the Qin Records.
The Story of the King of Vārāṇasī Awakening to the State of a Pratyekabuddha.
I take refuge in the World-Honored One, the All-Knowing, The Great Lamp of Illumination who fully comprehends the three periods of time;
I take refuge in the unsurpassed Dharma of definitive deliverance, And likewise in the noble Saṅgha of the Arhats.

I have heard of the Pratyekabuddhas who dwell in tranquility; They realize the practice of dependent origination, Their minds are free from blemish as they eliminate afflictions, And they skillfully guard the prohibitions and precepts, remaining ever pure.
Just as in autumn there are no clouds or veils, He dwells in solitude within the forest thickets;
Now, thirsting for and yearning after his merit, I sincerely revere and comply with him, giving rise to faith and joy.
Though I harbored doubts regarding what he desired, his power moved me so strongly that I was compelled to believe;
who, upon hearing of the pure and true conduct of a noble being, would not give rise to a mind of reverence and faith?
I shall now speak of a small portion of the merit and sublime conduct of the Pratyekabuddhas;
having heard this transmitted from former teachers, I shall relate only the authentic words without any false speech.
Just as when a great elephant walks upon a path, the young elephants follow, so do I now open and reveal it.
Question:

For what reasons and conditions does the Pratyekabuddha remain silent and maintain himself, entering a state of equanimity, dwelling in secluded places such as mountain forests, deep valleys, or riverbanks? Because his mental activities are tranquil, he likewise refrains from speech, practicing solitary conduct like that of a rhinoceros horn.
Why is this so? He asked again:
"What are the merits of a pratyekabuddha?"
The answer is:
The veteran masters of old all say this.
Formerly, when the Buddha was preaching the Dharma in the palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and was about to descend back to Jambudvīpa, he...

At that time, Śakra commanded Viśvakarman to construct three jeweled stairways for the Buddha to descend to Jambudvīpa; the lower pillars of these three stairways were situated in the kingdom of Saṃkaśya.
At that time, the Tathāgata descended from that celestial palace by way of a staircase; Śakra and Brahmā, together with their retinues, rained down flowers as an offering.

When the bhikṣuṇī Padmā saw the Buddha descending, she immediately manifested herself in the majestic form of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin), accompanied by the seven treasures and a ceremonial procession.
At that time, when the multitude beheld this, they were all filled with doubt and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, each saying:
"Is there perhaps anyone whose supernatural power is so transcendent and superior as to surpass that of this bhikṣuṇī?"

At that time, the World-Honored One saw that the assembled multitude was struck with wonder at the sight of the three stairways leading upward, and he also saw that the bhikṣuṇī Padmā had performed this supernatural feat, causing everyone to feel deep yearning and admiration. Desiring to increase their faith, he immediately addressed the assembly:
"There are pratyekabuddhas whose supernormal powers exceed those of this bhikṣuṇī."
What is meant by "superior"?
Those noble beings appear in the world even before a Buddha has appeared, acting for the benefit of all sentient beings.
They manifest physical forms and appear to experience hunger and thirst, accepting clothing and food to serve as fields of merit for others.

Adorning their practice of the Dharma with purity and tranquility, they tame themselves and become free from desire; thus, all sentient beings who behold them will have their evil intentions forever stilled and will lay down their swords and staves.
"It is like the solitary practice of the rhinoceros horn.
This was heard by the transmitter from various masters.
What was it that was heard?

I have heard that in the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a person who left the household life and practiced the holy life for ten thousand years, upholding the true precepts, cultivating patience, and remaining constantly diligent.
Because of his practice, many bhikṣus came to attend upon him.
At that time, all the bhikṣus spoke thus:
"Please instruct us."
Because they were habituated to such teachings, these bhikṣus all took delight in them.
Due to the clamor of the multitude, they were unable to see the Truth; at the time of their death, they formed this thought:
"I have seen the One of Ten Powers, whose Dharma teaching is subtle, profound, and far-reaching, and difficult to hear."
However, I have heard that because of negligence one does not attain the fruit of the Path.

Although I maintain pure precepts and am able to practice patience, because I teach and transform the clamor of the multitude, my concentrated mind is impaired; it is like frost and hail destroying the sprouts of goodness. Therefore, this causes me not to attain the fruit of the Path.
He then spoke in verse:
"I am now drowning in the three realms of existence, amidst a multitude of evils and afflictions,
like an old, emaciated elephant sunk deep in the mire."
Just as that Pratyekabuddha dwells alone in the forest,
like a rhinoceros with its single horn, remaining far removed from all followers;
one should practice in solitude, avoiding them as one would avoid a fierce, blazing fire.
"May I remain far removed from the clamor of crowds;
may I always stay aloof from the noisy bustle of factions.
Having made this vow, at the end of his life he was reborn in the heavens, where he experienced bliss.
When his merit was exhausted and his life came to an end, he was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of King Brahmadatta in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi.
At the time of his entry into the womb, the queen’s body was like a clear pond filled with delicate flowers.
At that time, having realized she was pregnant, the lady addressed the king with these verses:
“Since I have become aware of my pregnancy, Joy and a sense of grace have arisen within me.
This must surely be the aspiration of the child; It is fitting that those who have committed offenses be pardoned.”
When the king heard this, he was filled with joy and immediately granted a general amnesty throughout the realm.
He further addressed the king, saying:
"Furthermore, you ought to practice extensive giving."
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with even greater joy;
he immediately opened his treasuries to bestow gifts upon the poor and destitute, leaving none unsatisfied.

At that time, after the queen had given birth to the prince, he was exceptionally handsome and distinguished, like the full moon; when he reached the age of eight, he was intelligent, compassionate, and benevolent.
When his father, the king, passed away, the people loved and delighted in him as they would the full moon.
At that time, there was a minister named Vādin; the minister Vādin then installed the crown prince to succeed to the royal throne.
Although he was young in years, by the power of his original vows he committed no evil; his nature was noble and virtuous, and he possessed deep compassion for all sentient beings.

Though dwelling in the royal palace, his mind sought solitude; though residing in a magnificent hall, it was as if he were in a cemetery; though amidst the clamor and bustle, he practiced meditative contemplation. Loathing birth and death and weighing their faults, he cultivated his mind through the Way and renounced his royal duties.
The ministers remonstrated, saying:
"Today Your Majesty devotes yourself exclusively to the practice of the Way and neglects the affairs of state.
If this continues, many evils will surely arise and the royal customs and transformation will be ruined."
"It is like crossing the ocean: if there is no captain, one will surely be destroyed by various perils.
He then spoke in verse:
"The King inherits the ancestral succession, And has rightfully obtained the land as his domain."
Pray, govern the myriad people with principle and do not abandon the kingdom.
If the King rules according to the True Dharma and no good deed surpasses it,
O Lord of Men, you should know that protecting the kingdom brings the most supreme merit.
At that time, having heard these words, the king sighed and reflected, then spoke in verse as his reply:
"If I do not govern the kingdom, my realm will surely fall into ruin;
With my power, I am able to protect the land, so that the wicked of the borders dare not invade."
If I were to rule a kingdom, the affairs of kingship would only cloud my mind;
if there were those who committed crimes, I would surely inflict harm upon them,
saying they must be bound and imprisoned, or their hands and feet must be severed.
He should be sentenced to death; his eyes should be gouged out.
In this present age of turbidity and evil, he must certainly be executed.
One who carries out such execution is a *caṇḍāla*.
At that time, the king addressed his beloved ministers:
"Listen now: what I eat does not exceed a single flavor; what I wear does not exceed a single set of robes; and the place where I sit or lie down does not exceed the space required for my body."
Viewed from this perspective, why seek much and remain insatiable?

The reason the royal throne is called "honored" is that its commands must be carried out and there are none who do not receive them with reverence; it is solely because of this matter that it distinguishes itself from the common masses.
He further addressed the prime minister:
"This one matter alone is what a king values most; I now entrust it to you.

You must now stand in awe of future lives and govern the kingdom according to the True Dharma (Saddharma). As for taxes and levies, follow the established customs and do not exceed the regular limits."
He then spoke in verse:
"Though I was born in a royal palace And inherited the legacy of my ancestors,
I have not practiced the arts Of execution, flogging, or punishment."
Out of fear, I am now unable to perform this task;
do not follow my example, but rather nurture the common people.
All people in the world are ignorant and each commits their own transgressions.
Regarding the offenses you have committed, you should further give rise to a sense of dread.
You ought to nurture them with the True Dharma and bestow fearlessness;
relying upon the True Dharma, you should transform and guide the common people.
When the king had finished speaking these verses, he immediately entrusted the kingdom to this great minister.

Having obtained the kingdom, for two years the minister acted with unrestrained license; he showed no compassion for the myriad people, acting according to his own whims and committing various unrighteous acts. As time gradually passed, his position became so deeply entrenched that he gave rise to arrogance and negligence, performing further unrighteous deeds. Like a river in a violent flood, he caused great destruction, seizing all the wealth of the wealthy within the city by force.
At that time, the people within the city all admonished him, saying, "Do not do this.
Hearing these words of loyal counsel, his anger redoubled; with a frown and a contorted expression, he spoke these words:
"How dare you utter such words?
The people were struck with fear and did not dare respond to the king.

Consequently, his unrighteous conduct grew ever more rampant, like a fire that blazes even fiercer when it encounters dry fuel; his lustful, wanton, and violent transgressions became so audacious that he even abducted the wives of those he loved.
At that time, the King’s consort, seeing this, was overcome with grief and shed tears as she went to inform the King.
Her anger was so fierce that her lips and mouth quivered; her speech was indistinct, like that of an infant, as she related the matter in detail to the King.
Having heard this, the king immediately summoned him and said to him:
"If you, my queen, can still endure such things and commit what is contrary to the Dharma, how much more so will the myriad people?"
The king immediately admonished him, saying:
"From this day forward, do not act in such a manner again.

At that time, the prime minister, seeing that the king had grown weary of him and that the people were likewise disgusted, abandoned the kingdom and fled to another land. He then led the king of that other land and his military forces back toward his own country, intending to launch an invasion.
At that time, the former ministers of the kingdom led their troops to meet and resist him; they defeated his army and captured his men alive, bringing them back.
The former ministers and others again addressed the king, saying:
"That man has invaded and insulted Your Majesty."
He then led that minister to the king's presence.
At that time, seeing that the minister’s countenance had changed and bore an expression of shame and fear,
the king said:
"How strange is birth and death!
He then spoke this verse:
"The mind is shrouded by ignorance, Failing to perceive the great suffering that follows."
For the sake of a minor pleasure, one now endures this shame and disgrace.
It is like a superior, fine meal, complete in both color and fragrance, yet containing poison within; the fool does not perceive it.
"Because of their craving for flavor, they take food; once the food is digested, it becomes a source of harm.
The King said to his ministers:
"Although his transgression is indeed grievous, it is not my intention to inflict harm upon him."
He further spoke in verse:
"All cherish their own life; You should quickly pardon his offense.
For one has never seen anyone who, by harming another's life, Attained peace and happiness."
Toward those whose offenses are grave and heavy, one should instead give rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
Since they have brought this harm and injury upon themselves, one ought to feel compassion;
for if one were to take their life, one would destroy the very Dharma one holds dear.
The senior ministers then addressed the king, saying:
"Although we have now disobeyed Your Majesty’s decree, they will surely inflict harm upon us; we shall never let them go."
He immediately drew his sword before the king and struck him down.

Upon seeing him killed, the king felt a sense of revulsion; as he beheld the present realm, he perceived the past, and his mind of patience was instantly opened and liberated. He awakened to the path of a Pratyekabuddha, like the blooming of an utpala flower.
He leaped into the air, while all his ministers and attendants joined their palms and gazed upward.
"The Pratyekabuddhas who weary of birth and death realize the Way in this manner; such is the fruit of the precepts that I have now attained."
Then he spoke in verse:
"Though I wear jeweled necklaces, my mind cultivates pure brahmacarya;
I restrain the body and subdue the senses, remaining ever tranquil and detached."
"Among all people, he has laid aside the sword and staff;
he practices solitary conduct like the single horn of a rhinoceros.

When this verse was spoken, his hair and beard fell away of their own accord. At that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven presented him with a kāṣāya robe, and he immediately flew through the air to the Snowy Mountains.
At that time, there was a Pratyekabuddha on that mountain who asked him,
"While occupying the throne of a king, what did you find so loathsome that you awakened to this state of the Path?
He then replied by reciting the aforementioned verse.
Therefore, because sentient beings are unable to practice patience, the Tathāgata has taught the causes and conditions for patience.
Because they are attached to and frequent noisy, crowded places, he has taught the causes and conditions for not associating with such places.
In order to cause others to understand the merits of the pratyekabuddha, he spoke of the causes and conditions of the pratyekabuddha.
For the sake of the devas, the Buddha spoke of the causes and conditions of the pratyekabuddha in the Sudharmā Hall.
The Buddha, while in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, spoke of this matter in order to cause the devas to feel weary of and disgusted with worldly existence.
As for the Pratyekabuddha Vāsava, he preached at Vaiśālī that he would relinquish his body and enter parinirvāṇa; there is currently a stūpa existing there named Udayana.
Firmly maintaining the prohibitive precepts without violating their practice, those who possess wisdom attain liberation;
they do not learn from others nor do they afflict them, practicing in solitary solitude like the rhinoceros horn.
I have heard this teaching from various masters:

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who practiced the holy life for ten thousand years; through seated meditation he attained patience, maintained the prohibitive precepts, remained aloof from worldly clamor, and was fully endowed with the dhūta ascetic practices.
At the end of his life, he was reborn in the heavens, where he enjoyed the pleasures of the five senses within a celestial palace.
When his heavenly lifespan was exhausted, he was reborn in the womb of Devī, the wife of the prime minister of the city of Vatsa.
At that time, the lady spoke in verse to her husband:
"I am now pregnant; my heart is filled with great joy. Surely there shall be a person of merit who comes to be my son."
For this reason, I have given rise to compassion for all beings at all times.
Furthermore, my mind of negligence has now ceased and I no longer harbor desires; just as Mount Mahāmeru in the ocean can cut through the waves, so too is my desire now stilled.
I now fear false speech and constantly contemplate truthful speech; just as a virtuous person of merit fears any lapse, so too do I now exercise such careful apprehension.

I now view liquor as if beholding poisonous medicine, and I fear the wealth of others as if fearing a mass of fire; all such evils have now been entirely abandoned, solely due to me, the son of merit from her womb.
"Since sexual desire has been eliminated, how can it be used for pleasure?
At that time, the prime minister spoke to his wife, saying:
"Now, let your will be as you wish, and practice the five precepts."
At that time, the lady practiced various virtues, and when ten months had passed, she gave birth to a son whom she named Soma.

As he gradually grew up, he attained complete mastery in all the sūtras and śāstras as well as the sixty-four arts; he was so exceptionally handsome and sublime that he resembled the full moon, bringing perfect fulfillment to the desires of his parents.
When he reached his prime, the minister requested of the king:
"I am now old; for the sake of future lives, please allow me to cultivate merit.
At that time, the king replied:
"I cannot now create an obstacle to your cultivation of merit.
You may send your son Soma to take your place in providing for me; you are free to cultivate virtue."
The prime minister was filled with joy; the king appointed Soma as his new prime minister and bestowed upon him honors and rewards twice as great as those of his father.
The people loved and revered him, just as they had formerly revered the Great Minister Gavampati, who could inspire love and respect in all women.
At that time, the king’s consort was deeply attached to Soma and said to him:
"If you can now fulfill my wish, I shall be able to cause the entire kingdom, as well as the king himself, to follow you completely."
"Furthermore, I can ensure that you do not incur an ill reputation, and the instruction I provide will be no different from that of the King.
At that time, Soma, firm in his resolve and without fear, replied in verse:
"Please listen to what I have to say; do not look upon me with disdain or reproach."
When I heard these words, they sank into me like water soaking into the earth.
It was as if a weak horse, when exhausted and weary, were ridden into the midst of battle; it would be unable to press forward.
When I see another's wife, my mind is free from defilement; my heart remains unaroused, like a lotus flower at night.
Toward all those I revere, I feel no difference from feeling toward my own mother;
how much more so for this lady, who is one I hold in the highest honor.
I maintain a steadfast mind and serve those who are venerable with respect; as a minister and a son, I ought not to act in rebellion.
Furthermore, when my desires arise and I see another’s wife, they naturally subside.
"That torrential stream arises with many surging waves;
I am like the autumn water, naturally pure and clear.
At that time, the lady thought to herself:
"If he were to sever my affectionate ties, I would surely harbor slander toward him.
Thus she spoke to the king:
"The minister Soma has conceived an unreasonable intent, wishing to insult and humiliate me.
At that time, the king’s mind was bewildered with doubt, wondering whether this was indeed so or not.
At that time, Soma went to a garden grove and saw two oxen with yokes upon their necks, suffering from extreme exhaustion and distress; he felt a sense of revulsion.
Meanwhile, the King, who had been deluded by the slanderous words of his consort, immediately dispatched a messenger to kill Soma.
At that time, Soma was like a horse struck by an arrow that pierced right through to the bone; he immediately reflected:

"When a person is in a state of prosperity, all beloved objects of desire come before them, like food mixed with poison that is exceedingly fragrant and delicious, yet when one wishes to digest it, the body is utterly ruined."
Just as when a person craves the five desires, their flavor is exceedingly meager;
it is like a golden house that has been set on fire, where a person, craving its beauty, enters and is harmed, their mind becoming agitated and disturbed as life is about to end.
He immediately comforted himself and thought to himself:
"I maintain the pure precepts without any flaw or deficiency.
As for my observance of the precepts, I know them as well as the yak loves its tail."
"I maintain my prohibitive precepts just as a poor man who has discovered a hidden treasure in the earth guards it with diligent effort.
And he spoke in verse:
"The coarse, harsh, and treacherous path— I have already crossed over it."
Though I encounter urgent and perilous matters, I shall not abandon the precepts;
just as the tide of the great ocean does not miss its appointed time,
so too shall it be with my observance of the precepts now.
When these verses had been spoken, all the devas and benevolent spirits, seeing that the Prime Minister’s vow was such as this, were filled with joy.
At that time, various malevolent spirits immediately possessed the lady; she went mad, and being possessed by the spirits before the King, she spoke these verses:
“I am now utterly ruined; I must suffer death in this very body.”
He is a person of pure goodness; one should not inflict harm upon him.
Out of my childish ignorance, I blew at Mount Sumeru with my mouth, yet I could not cause it to shake.
"He was truly without any defiled conduct; I have falsely brought this slander upon him.

At that time, while reflecting with a sense of weary detachment within the garden, the prime minister attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha. He leaped up into the air, his hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven immediately offered him a kāṣāya robe.
At that time, the people entreated him, saying:
"We pray that you do not abandon us to ascend to the heavens.
Then the Pratyekabuddha answered the people with the verse mentioned above.
He flew to the Snowy Mountains and saw the various pratyekabuddhas, to whom he related the aforementioned matters in detail:
"The ocean tide does not overstep its limit; The yak dies guarding its tail.
Just as the nature of the moon is naturally cool, It cannot be changed to become hot."
One who has subdued the sense faculties guards the precepts in the same way;
this is called the solitary practice, like the rhinoceros horn, being without a second.
Thus have the great teachers of the past instructed one another in succession.
I have heard this from the former Victors, and now I wish to proclaim it clearly.

In a past age, there was a Pratyekabuddha named Candraprema (Moon-Love) who, under the Blessed One Kāśyapa Buddha, planted various roots of goodness and diligently cultivated the practice of the precepts. Constantly using wisdom, he contemplated that all the aggregates (*skandhas*) are entirely impermanent; yet, in the presence of that Buddha, he ultimately did not attain the fruits of the śramaṇa path.
Having passed away there, he was immediately reborn in the heavens, where he experienced celestial bliss through the power of his past merit.
When his heavenly lifespan ended, he descended back to the human world and was born into the family of a great elder in the kingdom of Campā.
From his youth, he was refined and elegant, constantly cultivating himself by relying on the precepts and prohibitions.

Observing his virtuous conduct, it surpassed that of long-standing elders; he was neither frivolous nor impulsive, and harbored no anger or resentment. He distributed all his wealth and resources to those in poverty, sharing whatever his household possessed—whether abundant or meager—with the community, adorning himself with the necklace of the precepts.
When his father passed away, he governed the household according to the Dharma.
The people of that city, seeing his loyalty and prudence, conceived deep respect and faith toward him as if he were their own teacher.

In the prime of his youth and possessing a handsome appearance, there was not one among the young women who did not fall in love with him upon seeing him; likewise, all the merchants and traders, moved by his sincerity, came to rely upon him.
At that time, there were several merchants from the north who traveled with many fine horses to the kingdom of Campā. King Campā seized all their horses.
The king’s mind was violent and cruel, and he did not rely on the True Dharma; he thought to himself:
"I have now taken many horses from them; how can I obtain these horses without paying their value?"
He immediately convened a council with his sycophantic ministers to deliberate on this matter. The sycophantic ministers addressed the king, saying:
"If you were to pay their price, the treasury would be completely exhausted.
The king then replied:
"If I do not pay the price now, my ill repute will spread throughout the world; all the people of the nation will suffer because of me, and furthermore, trade from the four quarters will be cut off."
The sycophantic minister spoke again:

"If one devises a plan for the King, it will be possible to obtain the horse without requiring wealth, and furthermore, ensure that the King’s ill repute does not spread among the people and that the subjects suffer no distress."
"Now, within Your Majesty's realm, the minister Candraprema is trusted and relied upon by all people.
If he comes to demand [the gold], Your Majesty should simply say:
'I have dispatched Candraprema to deliver the gold to you.'"
"At that time, that merchant had ten thousand horses, each horse being worth ten thousand gold coins.
If the King were to say merely, 'I shall give the price to Minister Candraprabha,' the people of the kingdom would surely become suspicious—some suspecting the King, others suspecting Candraprabha."
"The King's ill repute need not be made manifest, nor will it cause the myriad people to feel weary or distressed.
Then the merchants came and said to the King, "Return our price for the horses; we wish to return home."
The king replied,
"Did I not previously have Candraprabha pay you that price?
Would it not be better for me to give you the full value once again?"
The merchants replied to the king:
“As for this Candraprabha, from the very beginning he has indeed not paid us the price for the horses.
Yet, being loyal and trustworthy, he would rather sacrifice his own life than ever speak a falsehood regarding the payment of our price.”
He then spoke in verse:
"Suppose the moon were to rain fire, and the sun were to rain cool water;
suppose one could extract oil from pressing sand, or obtain clarified butter by drilling into water."
"For a lotus to grow within fire, or for that Moon-Lover to utter coarse and reckless falsehoods— such things can never come to pass.
The merchants then addressed the king again, saying:
“O Deva among Men!
Even if Candraprabha were truly to grant me as you have commanded, O King, I would never harbor resentment.
Thereupon, the King summoned Candraprabha and spoke to him, saying:
"Previously you were not here before me; shall I give you gold to repay the debt of a merchant?
The king then moved his eyes and manifested a deceitful expression, saying, "If you do not comply with me, I will certainly kill you."
At that time, the minister Candrapriya thought to himself:
"On this day, shall I follow the words of truth,
or shall I use the King's command?"
He further reflected to himself:
"Is the excellence of the Dharma-body superior,
or is this physical body superior?"
He then made a firm resolve:
"I would rather sacrifice this body now than ever abandon the Dharma-body of the precepts.
He then spoke a verse:
"I now reflect upon myself: between these two bodies, which one should I relinquish?
Furthermore, observing myself with clarity, I would rather cast away this base and defiled form than ever forsake the precepts."
If I were to abandon the Dharma-body, my ill repute would immediately spread abroad.
Since I am held in the hands of the multitude of the virtuous,
I would not personally find pleasure in being an evildoer.
The fire of remorse arises within the mind; having cast off this defiled body, one shall surely proceed to hell.
Having destroyed one’s own observance of the precepts, one shall never attain peace and happiness.
If one seeks pleasure for a single body, one brings ruin to an infinite body;
if one guards the precepts, the infinite body shall be at peace.
One protects the Dharma-body so that it may not be destroyed.
"For the sake of benefiting the True Dharma, one must sever all false speech.
The minister Candrapriya then addressed the king, saying:
"I pray that Your Majesty will show mercy and not be angry with me; I truly do not recall seeing Your Majesty give him that price."
At that time, the king became greatly enraged; he struck his sword and said, "How can you not see?
Then, the minister Candraprema resolved his mind and thought to himself:
"Better to die for the noble Dharma than to live in folly; among all beings who are born, who is there that does not die?
If I must now face death, let my body perish for the sake of the Dharma."
"I am certain to be reborn in the heavens; why should I feel fear or alarm?
He then replied to the king:
"Even if Your Majesty were to cut my body into pieces as small as sesame seeds this very day, I would never abandon the precepts I have received."
"Now that I abide in the path of the sages and saints, it would be unbecoming of me to utter a falsehood with this tongue.
If I were now to tell a lie for the sake of becoming king and subsequently fall into hell, what could I rely upon?"
At that time, the king’s shame increased tenfold and his anger flared; he glared at him with eyes like blazing fire.
Candraprabha then felt joy arise in his heart:
"Now is precisely the time for me to give rise to a fixed resolve; now is precisely the time for me to uphold the Dharma. Where else could I wish to seek the hearing of the Dharma?"
"Today he has preached the Dharma for me.
Today, for the sake of the Dharma, I am even willing to sacrifice my life; today, O King, you are truly my great friend.

Thinking thus of the Dharma, he immediately attained awakening and became a Pratyekabuddha. He leaped into the air so that those who had broken the precepts might see this and feel shame, so that those cultivating wholesome deeds might increase their faith and practice, and so that those who speak the truth might witness the fruits of reality.
In mid-air, his beard and hair fell away of their own accord, and the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven presented him with Dharma robes.
He flew to Mount Gandhamādana, where he gathered together with the pratyekabuddhas in one place and spoke the verses as above.
*Pratyekabuddha-nidāna-śāstra*, Volume Upper;
*Pratyekabuddha-nidāna-śāstra*, Volume Lower.
Translator unknown; now appended to the Qin Records.
The Story of the Great Elder of Rājagṛha Awakening to Pratyekabuddhahood:
It is like being in a dense forest where one wishes to pull out a great tree;
the branches and twigs obstruct one another, so that there is no way to find an exit.
The household life is like a dense forest; its myriad affairs are like its branches and twigs.
Though one may wish to seek the essential path of liberation, there is no cause for ever breaking free from bondage.
Dwelling in stillness within the forest wilds, observe the objects of perception and cultivate the mind.
Having liberated oneself from all worldly concerns and departed from all that is dear and beloved,
one cultivates the practice of solitary wandering like the rhinoceros horn,
without a second companion; this is what I have heard transmitted by my former teachers.

In the past, there was a Pratyekabuddha who had constantly cultivated various virtues under five Buddhas of the past; however, as a lay follower (upāsaka), he took pleasure in domestic affairs and, despite beholding those Buddhas, did not seek to leave the household life.
However, he concentrated his mind on observing the precepts for laypeople without any transgression.

His roots of goodness gradually increased, and he left the household life to study the Way under Kāśyapa Buddha. He delighted in practicing the dhūta austerities and was fully equipped with the six requisites; loathing sensual desires, he passed away there and was reborn in a celestial palace.

When his celestial lifespan came to an end, he was reborn in the household of a great elder in the city of Rājagṛha; this elder’s family possessed immeasurable wealth, and their storehouses were overflowing.
As he gradually grew up and reached the prime of youth, after his father passed away, he lived in accordance with his heart's delight, like Viśravaṇa’s son, Nalakūvara.

Within his own home, he delighted in various worldly affairs; he fathered and raised thirty sons and thirty daughters each, and his treasuries and servants were exceedingly numerous. With so many matters concerning the marriages of his sons and daughters, he busied himself only with the present, forgetting the Dharma he was meant to practice.

Bound by worldly affairs, he did not abandon his household duties; yet from his servants he heard that many of his relatives had met with death and loss, and that the house of the maiden so-and-so had not only suffered this calamity of mourning but had also lost its livelihood.
Hearing such reports of loss, he was filled with grief, anguish, and distress, as if a hundred arrows were piercing his heart all at once.
Yet he also heard pleasant, virtuous, and delightful words: that the family merchant had returned safely after acquiring great treasures, and that their son so-and-so had given birth to a boy.
Furthermore, hearing that his daughter has given birth to a son endowed with merit, he feels great joy;
yet hearing of the decline of his former prosperity, sorrow and joy mingle within him, like the wheel of a performing artist as it revolves.

Accompanied by a close friend, he went into a park; while wandering about for sightseeing, they arrived at a grove where he saw a man cutting down a great tree whose branches, twigs, and leaves were so dense and luxuriant that many elephants could not pull it out.
However, when he cut down a small tree that had no branches or twigs, a single person was able to pull it out of the grove without any difficulty.
Having seen this event, he reflected within himself and spoke these words:
"I have now encountered the necessary conditions.
He then uttered this verse:
"I see a great tree being felled, its branches and leaves exceedingly numerous;
entangled within the dense forest, there is no way to escape.
The world is just like this, with its men, women, and various kinsmen."
When the mind is bound by love and hatred, one cannot attain liberation from the dense forest of birth and death;
yet a small tree without branches and twigs cannot be obstructed by such a forest.
"Having severed all endearments, one attains liberation spontaneously from the dense forest of birth and death. Thereupon,
he attained the path of a Pratyekabuddha at that very spot.
Then that friend said to him:
"The sun is already setting; we should return home together.
He replied to his friend:
"Return home yourself;
my connection to the household has now been severed.
His friend asked:
"How have you severed it?
He replied, "In the past, I was attached to the household life because of craving; now I have already severed such karma of craving."

People are attached to their wives, children, and kinsmen; even toward their young sons and infant grandsons, they are indulgent out of affection. When they see their fathers, they do not cease their clamorous play but quickly run to cling to them; because they are so enamored with these things, they give rise to attachment.
Regarding my wife, children, and kinsmen, such attachments as these have forever ceased within me.

Formerly, when I lived at home managing various affairs, I would go out or come in, saying "give this to that person" or "take this from here," or saying "this should be done" or "this should not be done."

Such matters as these I have now severed; having abandoned sensual pleasure, I have attained the bliss of liberation; I have felled the root of the tree of craving, closed the gates to the various realms of existence, and extinguished the great obscuration of darkness.
"Regarding this infant, I am like an enemy; there is no difference between us.
Now that I am in such a state, how could I ever return home?
At that time, his kinsman and friend returned to the house and spoke to his sons and daughters.
When the men and women, both old and young, heard that he had not returned, they all went to see for themselves.
When their kinsmen arrived, they saw only their father, a śramaṇa in dharma robes, soaring into the void.
The man and woman said,
"By what matter do you now feel weary of and loathe your retinue?
Standing in mid-air, he immediately spoke the aforementioned verse in response to the man and woman.

Having spoken these verses, he immediately flew to the midst of the Snowy Mountains; after convening with the pratyekabuddhas there, he returned to the grove where he had originally attained the Way, cast off his body, and entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, his kinsmen constructed a stūpa and temple for him; because of this, people of the time named it the Bahuputra Stūpa.
Generally, when the roots of goodness of wise persons have matured, they attain awakening through even slight causes and conditions.
Wife, children, kinsmen, and wealth—these are the perils within the cycle of birth and death.
To dwell in the forest in silent liberation is like the single horn of the rhinoceros.
What I have heard from the Sugata has been transmitted to my teacher.
I have further heard this from my teacher, and I shall now expound it for you.

In the past, there was a Pratyekabuddha who practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) under Kāśyapa Buddha for twelve thousand years. He constantly cultivated patience and compassion toward sentient beings, never violating even the most minor precepts, and upon the end of his life, he was reborn in heaven.

When his life in that heaven came to an end, he was reborn in the human world into the family of the king of Vārāṇasī. He was born at the time of the moon’s rising, and for this reason he was named Candrodaya.
As he gradually grew up, he was established as the crown prince; upon the death of his father the king, he succeeded to the throne.
By virtue of his past roots of goodness, he ruled the kingdom as a King of the True Dharma. He dispatched the son of a minister to govern a minor state and gave him his daughter in marriage.
This son of the minister possessed peerless valor and strength and had many kinsmen; however, relying on his own pride and arrogance, he behaved with excessive insolence.
At that time, the prince was extremely close with the son of the prime minister, who was the husband of his sister.
Taking advantage of their private and secluded leisure, the minister secretly hatched a slanderous plot and said to the prince:
"Your uncle has many brothers and kinsmen, yet worldly people often give credence to the words of women."
Once your royal father has suddenly fallen, your various mothers may give rise to slander and flattery, each favoring their own son.
Judging by this, the position of your father’s kingship will certainly not reach you.
Before King Man awakens, it is fitting that you act against him early.

For the royal throne is the most honored position in the world; its ultimate bliss is no different from that of heaven, and there is not a single person among all the world’s inhabitants who does not believe in and submit to it.
If one serves as a sovereign of a nation and governs by means of the Dharma, after the end of life, one will certainly be reborn in heaven.
For example, just as all people crave fine meat, so too is the position of kingship—there is no one who does not covet it.
He then spoke in verse:
"Just as when the water has not yet arrived, One should strive to construct a bridge;
If a torrential flood should suddenly come, There will be nothing that can be done."
The royal throne is likewise; you should plan for it first.
Once he is captured within your grasp, only then may you find peace.
If brothers harbor mutual jealousy, it will be extremely difficult to seek him out later.
The prince reflected:
"This is surely intended to cast me down, like ashes covering a blazing fire;
there is no pleasure in the present, and in the future one will encounter great suffering."
At that time, the prince reported all these matters in detail to his father, the King.
Upon hearing his son’s words, the King knit his brows and glared with eyes like red copper.
At that moment, the King issued a command to his messenger, saying:
"Before his semen has been discharged, you must pursue him quickly and bring him back.
When the prince heard that the son of the chief minister had arrived, he immediately went out to meet him.
Once they had met, the prince was immediately stricken by an ailment.
The messenger returned and reported to the king, saying,
"The prince’s illness has become so severe that he has fallen into a state of extreme debility.
Upon hearing this, the king immediately went out to see him.
Having seen that his son was gravely ill and in a perilous state, suffering from the pains of the four elements,
he reflected upon this and thought:
"This royal throne is truly a great evil."
However, that minister and his son have secretly instructed my son to act in defiance of the natural order of heaven, intending to commit an act of rebellion.
Yet this royal throne of mine cannot be obtained by them.
"My son now suffers from grievous illness and his life hangs by a thread; all people of the world give rise to greed and envy.
From this, one should know that the position of kingship is a base, contemptible, and wretched state."

Why is it base and depraved? Because for the sake of royal power one abandons virtuous conduct; for the sake of royal power one harms one’s father and grandfather; for the sake of close associates one commits great transgressions and evils; one abandons shame and modesty, which leads to arrogance and indolence; and for the sake of minor pleasures, one does not fear the future world.
He then spoke in verse:
"Just as a moth throws itself into a blazing fire, so too is the blind man who craves a kingdom;
deeply attached to gain and loss, he is concerned with what has been done and what has not been done."
Sunk in the mire of worldly affairs, one cannot find the state of tranquil concentration.
When one reflects in this way, bodily conduct becomes utterly pure;
having attained a mind of weary detachment, one immediately realizes the state of a Pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, another master says:
After this king saw his son’s affliction, he immediately returned to the palace.
At that time, a neighboring king with whom he shared a close and friendly bond was being oppressed by bandits; he dispatched an envoy to request assistance.
Upon hearing this, that king immediately led his troops to rescue the other king.
Having arrived in that country, the armies engaged in combat with blades clashing; they slaughtered one another most brutally, even tearing out and killing infants within the wombs of women.
When the king witnessed this event, he conceived a profound sense of revulsion toward his royal station and immediately spoke these verses:
"Out of greed for the trivial pleasures of the kingdom, One sinks into the mire of desire;
As lust and anger increase, Conflict gives rise to right and wrong."
For the sake of greed for wealth and profit, they mutually slaughter one another;
seeking neither supreme liberation nor the preservation of their royal thrones,
they perish like moths flying into a great blazing fire.
How strange! Within the cycle of birth and death, one’s actions are inverted;
exerting oneself with extreme toil, one instead reaps bitter calamity.
It is like that on the peak of a high mountain, where a honeybee dwells by the cliffside.
"The fool craves a little taste, yet does not perceive the suffering of falling.
Thus reflecting within himself, he immediately attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha.
He then addressed his son, saying:

“Since you are able to disregard the words of wicked men and harbor no rebellious intent, and since you will surely govern the kingdom with the True Dharma, I now entrust this kingdom to you; I am about to depart.”
When the prince, the prime minister, and all their retinue heard these words of the king, they were all overcome with grief; shedding tears and weeping, they joined their palms and said to the king:
"We do not know, Great King, where you intend to go?"
At that time, the father-king leaped into the air atop Mount Sunrise and recited the aforementioned verses; clad in the robes of a śramaṇa, he performed eighteen kinds of miraculous transformations.

Among the people of the land, there were none who did not rejoice upon seeing him; just as a well-trained horse becomes docile at the mere sight of the whip’s shadow, so too does the wise person become compliant and disciplined upon seeing others undergo suffering.
Parents, wife, and children, grain, silks, wealth, and treasures—
the wise observe these deeply as merely transient, like a guesthouse;
they abandon craving and desire, wandering alone like a rhinoceros horn.
In the past, I received this account through the oral transmission of various masters.

Formerly, there was a bhikṣu who had served under Kāśyapa Buddha; he was wise, intelligent, gentle, and patient. Day after day, he constantly contemplated the true nature of all phenomena—namely, that the aggregates (skandhas) are suffering, empty, impermanent, and non-self, being like a plantain tree, a mirage in the heat, an illusion, a dream, or a bubble on the water.
Being able to skillfully observe and cultivate his own mind, he was reborn in heaven after his life ended.
When his celestial lifespan was exhausted, he descended to be born in the city of Kauśāmbī as the prince of the kingdom, named Mahārāja.

When his father, the king, passed away, he succeeded to his predecessor’s legacy and inherited the royal throne, just as the kings at the beginning of the kalpa had well-cultivated their moral conduct and governed the country by the True Dharma.
At that time, there was a great elder in the city whose wealth was immeasurable; he had been a close friend of the great king since their youth, and they were extremely intimate with one another.
That great householder was afflicted with a grave illness; when the king heard of his sickness, he went in person to inquire after him.
Seeing the householder’s diseased form, withered and emaciated, the king’s heart was ill at ease; he lowered his head in sorrowful dejection.
At that time, the elder filled a bowl made of the seven precious gems with refined gold and presented it to the king.
The king said to the elder,
"Are you now suffering from illness so severely that you are in extreme distress?"
The householder replied:
"I pray that Your Majesty will deign to look upon me and listen to what I have to say.
My family is immensely wealthy, just like Vaiśravaṇa."
With kind words and material wealth, I gathered a great multitude of friends and kin;
wives, children, and retinues, as well as servants and messengers—
I allowed them all their desires and treated them with the utmost generosity.
"Now the time of my death has arrived, and not a single person shall be my companion.
The king then comforted him, saying:
"Your son and your kinsmen, your wealth, treasures, and all your storehouses—"
And my own heroic strength— elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—
though I possess such as these, none are able to rescue you. We, your many kinsmen and friends,
seeing you encounter this suffering and affliction, [are powerless].
There are only words of consolation, while you grieve and shed tears;
when your life is about to end, there is no one who can rescue you.
You must rely solely upon yourself and the wholesome deeds you have performed throughout your life.
The King observed his illness with a mind like that of one who has attained dhyāna;
he deeply realized the nature of all suffering and afflictions, and that they are certain to exist for sentient beings.
"All classes of living beings must inevitably succumb to illness."
Sickness constantly afflicts and torments people, yet it possesses no heart of compassion.
All people in the world are certain to enter the path of death,
yet they feel neither revulsion nor fear, saying, "This is my wife and child."
"That one is my relative, this is my wealth;
that one is kind to me, I am a friend to that one.
Afflicted by the delusion of the mind, one falsely forms such conceptions.
"The calamity of fire stands before me, yet I am foolish and blind and do not see it;
among all my kinsmen who have come to me, there is none who can rescue me.
As he reflected correctly upon this, he immediately attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha.

The king’s close relatives, both internal and external, seeing that the king had attained the Way and utterly abandoned worldly affairs, were scorched by the fire of separation from those they loved and gave rise to great anguish and feverish distress.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha ascended into the air, performed the eighteen kinds of miraculous transformations, and recited the verse mentioned above.
Furthermore, there is another account which says:
when this king was still a prince, he entered a garden grove and saw several blind men holding one another's hands.
Hearing that the prince was coming out, they thought there would be food and drink by the side of the road.
Not seeing the path, they fell into a great, deep pit; some died on the spot, some had their heads shattered, some had their hands and feet broken, and others had their bodies crushed to pieces.
At that time, the prince, seeing these manifold sufferings, became weary and contemplative, and spoke these words:
"This has awakened me.
Even such a blind man was once wealthy and noble, yet due to his indulgence in negligence, he now endures this suffering."
"Having now witnessed this matter, I ought to examine my conduct well; I must not be negligent.
He then spoke in verse:
"Just as fire burns a golden wreath, yet it is used as an ornament for the head,"
Though a golden garland be precious and exquisite, blazing fire ultimately brings harm;
sovereignty is likewise—be cautious and do not be negligent.
This blind man has awakened me; I ought not to be self-indulgent.
Because of this royal throne, one gives rise to great arrogance;
by intimidating the people of the kingdom, one causes them all to suffer distress.
When suffering comes to oneself later, that pain will be a hundred thousand times more intense.
Beholding others suffering before my very eyes, how could I find peace for myself?
This one is my teacher; he has shown me the manifold afflictions of suffering.
While reflecting thus, I immediately attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha.
At that time, the prince bestowed great wealth, money, and precious jewels upon the blind man.
Dressed in the dharma-robes of a śramaṇa, he ascended into the air and manifested various supernatural transformations. He spoke to his kinsmen, saying:

"It is not because of anger, fear, or sorrow, nor because I hold you in contempt, that I have renounced my kin, my kingdom, and its people; I am now entirely free from enmity or affection, and from money, wealth, and treasures."
As stated above in verse:
"Playful laughter and all objects of pleasure are cast aside like mucus and spittle;
one finds joy in renunciation and brings an end to all sufferings."
Having exhausted craving, attachment, and delusion, his mind has attained liberation;
because he has attained liberation, he dwells alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
This was heard by me from a former teacher.
In the past, there was a Pratyekabuddha who had cultivated various roots of goodness under former Buddhas; in his final birth, he was born in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī and became the king of Kauśāmbī.
Within that land there were great calamities and transformations: a severe drought, malicious winds, and the five planets were in disarray.
The king summoned the court astrologers and diviners and, speaking in verse, asked them:
"For what cause do these disasters exist? Why does the great drought not send down rain?"
In a sky free from clouds and mists, the sun appears devoid of its majestic radiance;
carnivorous birds of ill omen— crows, vultures, owls, and screech-owls—
soar high through the void, striking terror into those who behold them.
All said: "Such a calamity as this—by whom was it wrought, that these various demons and anomalies could cause such strange transformations?
At that time, the Grand Astrologer replied to the King:
"I shall now speak according to what I know.
As it appears to me, all the subjects of the kingdom will surely experience matters of oppression and suffering.
The king asked again:
"By what means should this calamity be averted?
The Grand Astrologer replied,
"If Your Majesty wishes to bring peace and security to the kingdom, you must follow my instructions."
Then he spoke in verse:
“If the King can abdicate his throne, Cast off his robes for others,
And for a full six months, Walk about in humble attire begging for alms,”
"Calamities shall naturally be eliminated; Your Majesty should be like the full moon.
Following these words, the king immediately abdicated his throne and traveled through the kingdom in humble attire.
Gradually traveling on, he arrived at the city of Bāhika.
Upon reaching that city, a king of another kingdom raised an army to invade; for the sake of his nation’s welfare, the King of Bāhika mobilized his troops to go forth and resist him.
As the two armies engaged in battle, both kings perished; the princes of the city of Bāhīka vied with one another to seize the kingdom and fought a great war once more.
When the seer-king Vīra witnessed this, he cried out in lamentation, "How strange! and spoke this verse:
"Though the royal throne be noble and majestic, its pleasures are exceedingly slight."
For what reason do they undergo all manner of bitter suffering?
With a competitive mind, they give rise to strife;
delighting in and clinging to various evils, they are like flies greedy for honey—clinging to the honey, there is nothing they do not lose.
Human beings are also like this: for the sake of a small pleasure, they fight and bring harm upon themselves.
They accumulate many sufferings and afflictions until, through these calamities, they reach their destruction.
Like drinking a potion mixed with poison, when the poison is digested, the body perishes.
For the sake of one's own person, many injuries are inflicted;
the fool craves the pleasures of kingship, yet the pleasure is slight while the suffering is immense.
From this day forth I shall forever cease; I no longer seek such pleasures.
For the affairs of this kingdom are filled with anxiety and fear;
while its glory and joy last but a moment, its sorrows and afflictions endure for long.
It is like a house of exquisite gold, Whose flames burn with fierce intensity;
The wise, fearing the harm of the fire, Should not enter within it.
While reflecting in this way, He immediately realized the state of a Pratyekabuddha.
By the power of his supernormal faculties, his beard and hair fell away naturally;
he immediately assumed the form of a śramaṇa, leaped into the air,
and while suspended in mid-air, he spoke the verses mentioned above.
He immediately flew to where the various pratyekabuddhas were in the Snowy Mountains.
At that time, those pratyekabuddhas asked him:
"By what causes and conditions have you attained the fruit of the Way?"
He replied with the aforementioned verses:
"All worldly amusements and pleasures, as well as attachment to 'I' and 'mine,' have been entirely cast aside; my mind has attained liberation."
All his faculties are utterly tranquil, He wanders alone like a rhinoceros horn.
In the past, I heard this account From my former teacher: Long ago, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Priyārūpa.

He had two queens whom he loved dearly; they were deeply attached to sensual pleasures, constantly indulging in negligence, and as intoxicated by their desires as if drunk. They were like the wild elephants of Mount Gandhamādana, who, when the scent flows forth, enter Mount Mālina to indulge in their lustful ways.
At that time, the two ladies were envious of one another and each watched for the other's vulnerability.
One of the ladies then gave poison to her trusted confidant, who carried the medicine and gave it to the other lady.
The first queen, having taken the medicine, lay down in a state of madness and delirium; suffering extreme agony, she soon passed away.
When the second queen saw that she had died, she feigned grief, tearing her hair and beating her breast as she wailed, so that the entire palace was filled with sorrow and lamentation.
When the king heard of her death, he was overcome with great anguish.
All the attendants and servants of the queen tore off the necklaces and ornaments that adorned their bodies, smeared their limbs with dust, and were consumed by grief and sorrow.
Just as a flock of geese is pursued by a hawk, or as the daughters of the nāgas are terrified by the garuḍa, so too are the court ladies in the palace struck with terror by death.
At that time, the palace was like a cemetery, and like dark dust obscuring the light; the various palace ladies were likewise overwhelmed by grief.
Hearing such words of grief and suffering from the palace women, the king’s heart was deeply shaken; he cast his celestial crown, necklaces, and all his royal attire to the ground.
He entered the place of mourning and beheld the palace ladies, whose expressions of sorrow and anguish reached their ultimate limit.
Having seen this, the king was overcome with great sorrow and anxiety; he reflected within himself and spoke these verses:
"Just as the scorching heat of midsummer sun can wither even the finest flowers, so does the day of death dissolve the human form, turning the complexion a sickly blue-black."
Their lips and teeth are stained with grime; their eyes are sunken and their noses are crooked.
Though they once possessed exquisite grace in song and dance, they now stand as rigid as wood or stone.
Those who came before were able to lead me to a state of deep attachment toward the realm of ultimate bliss.
Why does it suddenly today produce such fear in me?
The affliction of birth and death is loathsome, impure, and utterly foul;
it is as empty and unreal as a dream, and like the core of a plantain tree.
Lacking any mark of solidity, like an illusion, a bubble, a flame, or foam,
appearing for a moment like ripples on water, they are what the wise loathe.
Those who do not know how to observe them give rise to false notions of pleasure and attachment.
"Amidst this impurity, one falsely gives rise to the notion of a body;
bewildered and deluded, one clings to it like a sleeper.
While he was reflecting thus, before long, the funeral rites for the queen’s corpse were completed.
The second wife, wishing to conceal her own transgressions, ate fine food while feigning distress and declaring her intention to fast, manifesting an appearance of deep sorrow.
However, fearing that her faults would be exposed and discovered, she remained bound by anxiety within her heart.
Because of this knot of grief, his food and drink were not digested, and he immediately fell gravely ill.
Upon seeing his illness, the king’s distress redoubled; he conceived a sense of revulsion, realizing that all such things are the faults and afflictions of birth and death.
Then he spoke in verse:
"Just as a woman can give rise to love, The burdens she produces are exceedingly numerous;
Among humans, there is none who is not thus, For from love, pleasure is born."
Yet again, great evil arises; craving is the root of suffering.
When one sees the union of craving and its objects, one must know this is impermanent.
That which I love and delight in—my comely form and my prime of youth—[are likewise impermanent].
Once death has gathered [its hosts], one should know for this reason:
how could there be such pleasure?
What person of wisdom would give rise to joy and delight at the time of being united with those they love?
"Fearing the afflictions of old age, sickness, and death, I have therefore forever departed from them.
While he was reflecting thus, he immediately attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha.
He then donned royal garments and necklaces, ascended into the air, and while suspended in mid-air, spoke the verse above.
He transformed into a śramaṇa and flew to the place where the pratyekabuddhas were dwelling in the Snowy Mountains. 9.

The Story of the Youngest Son of a Universal Monarch Awakening to Pratyekabuddhahood: The Story of the Youngest Son of a Universal Monarch Awakening to Pratyekabuddhahood. In the past, immeasurable kalpas ago, there was a universal monarch (cakravartin rāja) who possessed a full thousand sons.

The youngest son saw his father mounted upon the precious golden wheel, complete with the seven treasures, escorted by the fourfold army, and fully adorned with drums, parasols, and ornaments. Thereupon, the youngest son asked his mother:
"When shall I too obtain such various adornments as these parasols and the rest?"
The mother replied,
"Even when your bones have rotted away, you shall not obtain this.
The son then asked:
"Why can you not obtain it? [He replied:
"You have nine hundred and ninety-nine elder brothers who should succeed to the throne.
Calculating according to the proper order, it does not reach you at all."
The boy then reflected:
"Since I cannot obtain such beauty and adornment, birth must inevitably lead to death and the decay of the physical form.

Through these various reflections on the faults and sufferings of birth and death, he immediately attained awakening and became a Pratyekabuddha; his body ascended into the air and performed the eighteen transformations.
The mother then requested again, "I pray that you do not go far away; please stay in this garden and accept my offerings.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha accepted the mothers' request and stayed in the rear garden, where he was provided for daily for a long period of time.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha, weary of this physical body, immediately cast it aside and entered nirvana.

His mothers, filled with longing remembrance, piled up a great quantity of fragrant wood to cremate his body; they collected his relics, placed them in a precious vase, and erected a great stupa in the rear garden.
At that time, when the Wheel-Turning King returned from his tour of the four cities and reached the rear garden, he saw a great stupa and asked about it in wonder.
The garden keeper then addressed the king, saying:
"This is the youngest son of Your Majesty who attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha and entered parinirvāṇa here; the mothers have erected this stupa for him."
Then the Wheel-Turning King summoned his mother and asked her,
"How did my son die that this stupa was built?
At that time, his mother and the others related the aforementioned events in detail to the king.
The king rebuked his mother, saying:
"My son desired this; why did you not tell me?
Although he has now entered nirvana, I shall place royal ornaments upon his stupa."

"By reason of these causes and conditions, for immeasurable kalpas he has constantly been a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), and the natural merit he enjoys remains inexhaustible even to this day.
Had he remained within the cycle of birth and death, he would have served as a Wheel-Turning Sage King for two thousand five hundred lifetimes."
Because he had attained Buddhahood, he received two thousand five hundred precious parasols.

King Ajātaśatru offered five hundred precious parasols to the Buddha; the Licchavi of Vaiśālī offered five hundred precious parasols to the Buddha; the Sāgara Dragon King offered five hundred precious parasols to the Buddha; the Asura King also offered five hundred precious parasols to the Buddha; and Śakra, Lord of the Devas, likewise offered five hundred precious parasols to the Buddha. At that time, the World-Honored One accepted none of them.
Why is this? Should future disciples lack the provisions of food and clothing for their support, by the power of this merit, humans and devas shall naturally provide for them.
For this reason, one should know that the field of merit of the worthy and holy ones is profound, vast, and immeasurable.
The Treatise on the Causes and Conditions of Pratyekabuddhas, Volume II.
